Moral, Ceremonial, Judicial Law
MOR-ul ser-uh-MOH-nee-ul joo-DISH-ul
noun phrase (Reformed theology)
The Reformed-confessional threefold division of the Mosaic law into moral law (the Ten Commandments, perpetually binding), ceremonial law (the ritual-sacrificial-typological law, abrogated in Christ), and judicial law (the civil law of national Israel, expired except for its general equity). Westminster Confession XIX.

📖 Biblical Definition

The Reformed-confessional threefold division of the Mosaic law, articulated in Westminster Confession XIX. (1) The moral law: summarized in the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20; Deuteronomy 5), it expresses God's perpetual moral will, binds all people in all ages, and continues as the rule of righteousness for both the unbeliever (whom it condemns) and the believer (whom it guides, the third use). The moral law is grounded in God's unchanging holy character and was written on the heart at creation (Romans 2:14-15); it is not abrogated but fulfilled and established by Christ (Matthew 5:17-19; Romans 3:31). (2) The ceremonial law: the ritual, sacrificial, dietary, purity, and festival laws that typologically foresignified Christ and His work; these were a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ (Colossians 2:17; Hebrews 10:1), and are abrogated in Christ, who fulfilled and thereby ended them (Hebrews 8-10; the dietary laws set aside, Mark 7:19; Acts 10). (3) The judicial (civil) law: the civil-legal code given to Israel as a national-theocratic body (laws of property, courts, punishments, civil order); these expired together with the State of that people, not obliging any other now, further than the general equity thereof may require (Westminster XIX.4). The substantive principle of general equity: while the specific Israelite-theocratic applications have expired, the underlying just principles (general equity) continue to inform the civil order. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive threefold division: the moral law is perpetually binding; the ceremonial law is abrogated in Christ; the judicial law has expired except for its general equity. The threefold division is essential for rightly handling the Mosaic law in the Christian life, distinguishing what continues (the moral law, the general equity of the judicial law) from what is abrogated (the ceremonial law, the specific Israelite-theocratic judicial applications).

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Reformed-confessional threefold division of the Mosaic law: moral (Ten Commandments, perpetually binding), ceremonial (ritual-typological, abrogated in Christ), judicial (civil law of national Israel, expired except for general equity); Westminster XIX.

MORAL, CEREMONIAL, JUDICIAL LAW, n. phr. (Reformed theology) The threefold division of the Mosaic law (Westminster XIX). (1) Moral law: the Ten Commandments; expresses God's perpetual moral will; binds all people in all ages; grounded in God's unchanging character (Romans 2:14-15); fulfilled and established (not abrogated) by Christ (Matthew 5:17-19). (2) Ceremonial law: ritual, sacrificial, dietary, purity, festival laws typologically foresignifying Christ; a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ (Colossians 2:17); abrogated in Christ (Hebrews 8-10; Mark 7:19; Acts 10). (3) Judicial/civil law: the civil code of national-theocratic Israel; expired together with the State of that people... further than the general equity thereof may require (Westminster XIX.4).

📖 Key Scripture

Matthew 5:17-18 — "Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil. For verily I say unto you, Till heaven and earth pass, one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled."

Colossians 2:16-17 — "Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days: Which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ."

Hebrews 10:1 — "For the law having a shadow of good things to come, and not the very image of the things, can never with those sacrifices which they offered year by year continually make the comers thereunto perfect."

Romans 13:8-10 — "Owe no man any thing, but to love one another: for he that loveth another hath fulfilled the law... Love worketh no ill to his neighbour: therefore love is the fulfilling of the law."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The threefold division is essential for rightly handling the Mosaic law; errors arise from collapsing the categories (treating all Mosaic law as either wholly binding or wholly abrogated) rather than distinguishing the perpetual moral law from the abrogated ceremonial and expired judicial.

expand to see more

The threefold division of the Mosaic law is essential for rightly handling the law in the Christian life, and errors arise from collapsing the categories. The antinomian error treats all the Mosaic law (including the moral law) as abrogated in Christ, leaving the believer with no abiding moral standard; this contradicts Christ's affirmation that He came not to destroy but to fulfill the law (Matthew 5:17-19) and the NT's continuing affirmation of the moral law (Romans 13:8-10; the apostolic citations of the Ten Commandments). The legalistic and the Judaizing error treats all the Mosaic law (including the ceremonial law) as perpetually binding, requiring Christians to keep the dietary laws, the festivals, circumcision, etc.; this contradicts the NT's clear teaching that the ceremonial law is abrogated in Christ (Colossians 2:16-17; Hebrews 8-10; the Jerusalem Council, Acts 15). The Reformed-confessional threefold division holds the substantive distinctions: the moral law (the Ten Commandments) is perpetually binding; the ceremonial law is abrogated in Christ who fulfilled it; the judicial law has expired with national Israel except for its general equity. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive division as the key to rightly handling the Mosaic law — honoring the perpetual moral law, recognizing the fulfilled-and-abrogated ceremonial law, and applying the general equity of the judicial law to the civil order.
